title: Rhythm and Time
bigQuestion: How can a pattern in time, repeated over and over, make people want to move?

story.title: The Warehouse and the Steady Kick
story.kicker: In Chicago in the late 1970s and early 1980s, a club and its DJ helped start a new kind of music built on a steady beat.
paragraphs: In the late 1970s, a club called the Warehouse opened on the West Side of Chicago. Its DJ was Frankie Knuckles. He did not just play records one after another. He blended them, stretched them and added beats so the dancing never had to stop.

Knuckles and other Chicago DJs began using drum machines under their records. A drum machine never gets tired and never speeds up by accident. It can play a kick drum on every beat, thump, thump, thump, thump, all night long. Dancers could lock onto that pulse and move together.

People started calling the music by the club's name. It became house music. From Chicago it spread to Detroit, to New York, to London and around the world. Much of the dance music on the radio today still stands on that steady kick.

Why does a steady beat feel so good? What is a beat, really, and how does a machine keep time so exactly? In this chapter you will measure rhythm with numbers: beats per minute, bars, and the sixteen steps of a drum machine.
story.think: Think of a song that makes you tap your foot. What part of the song is your foot following?

lessons.title: A Beat Is a Repeating Event
lessons.mainIdea: A beat is an event that repeats at an even spacing in time, like a clock's tick.
reading: Listen to a clock. Tick, tick, tick. Each tick is an event, and the time between ticks is always the same. When something repeats at an even spacing, it has a *beat*. The steady feeling underneath the beat is called the *pulse*.

Your body is full of beats. Your heart beats. You breathe in and out. When you walk, your feet land left, right, left, right at a fairly even pace. Music takes this idea and makes it something to share. Everyone can feel the same pulse and move with it.

A beat is a lot like a wave. Both repeat. A wave repeats in space and time, and a beat repeats in time. The time from one beat to the next is the beat's period, the same idea you met with sound waves. A slow song has a long period between beats. A fast song has a short one.

words.d: an event that repeats at an even spacing in time
the steady feeling of the beat underneath music

look.title: The Dripping Faucet
look.text: A faucet drips into a sink. Drip ... drip ... drip. You time it: one drip every second, again and again. Then someone turns the handle a little and the drips come twice as often.
look.prompt: Does the faucet have a beat? What happened to the period between drips when the handle turned?

check.q: What makes something a beat?
choices: It is played on a drum
It repeats at an even spacing in time
check.why: A beat is any event that repeats evenly, like a clock tick.

check.q: Which of these has a beat?
check.why: Your heart repeats at a fairly even pace, so it has a beat.

check.q: A song's beats come closer together. What happened to the period?
check.why: Beats closer together mean less time between them, a shorter period.

lessons.title: Tempo in Beats per Minute
lessons.mainIdea: Tempo is the speed of the beat, measured in beats per minute (BPM).
reading: How fast is the beat? Musicians call the speed of the beat the *tempo*. They measure it by counting how many beats fit in one minute. That unit is *beats per minute*, or BPM. A clock that ticks once a second is at 60 BPM.

BPM makes the math simple. At 60 BPM, each beat lasts one second. At 120 BPM, twice as many beats fit in the minute, so each beat lasts half a second. You can always find the time for one beat: divide 60 seconds by the BPM.

Different kinds of music tend to use different tempos. Slow songs might sit near 70 BPM. Many hip hop tracks sit roughly between 85 and 100 BPM. House music is often around 120 to 130 BPM. The Drum Machine has a tempo control, so you can hear the same pattern slow and fast.

words.d: the speed of the beat in a piece of music
the number of beats that fit into one minute, written BPM

look.title: How Long One Beat Lasts
look.cite: Worked out as 60 divided by BPM, rounded
look.prompt: As the BPM goes up, what happens to the time for each beat? Work out the time for one beat at 100 BPM.

check.q: What does BPM measure?
choices: How many notes are in the song
How many beats fit into one minute
check.why: BPM means beats per minute, the tempo.

check.q: At 120 BPM, how long is one beat?
check.why: 60 seconds divided by 120 beats is 0.5 seconds per beat.

check.q: A song speeds up from 90 BPM to 120 BPM. What happens to each beat?
choices: Each beat lasts a shorter time
Each beat gets lower in pitch
check.why: More beats in a minute means each one is shorter.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Measuring Tempo Yourself
lessons.mainIdea: You can measure a song's tempo by counting beats for a set time and scaling up to one minute.
reading: You do not need a machine to find a tempo. You need a clock and your ears. Start a timer, tap along with the beat, and count taps for 15 seconds. Multiply by 4, because a minute holds four sets of 15 seconds. That is your *estimate* of the BPM.

Any single count can be a little off. You might start tapping late or lose one beat. Scientists handle this by repeating a *measurement* and comparing. Count three times. If you get 29, 30 and 30 in 15 seconds, the tempo is about 120 BPM. The results agree, so you can trust them more.

You can measure other rhythms the same way. Find your pulse on your wrist and count for 15 seconds. Count a friend's steps as they walk. Count the chirps of a cricket on a summer night. Every repeating event has a tempo you can measure.

words.d: a careful, close guess based on measuring or reasoning
a number found by comparing something to a standard unit, such as seconds or beats

look.title: Three Tries
look.text: Maya taps along to a song for 15 seconds three times. She counts 24 taps, 23 taps and 24 taps. Her friend guesses the tempo is 60 BPM without counting.
look.prompt: What tempo do Maya's counts point to? Whose answer do you trust more, and why?

check.q: You count 30 beats in 15 seconds. What is the tempo?
check.why: Multiply 30 by 4 to scale 15 seconds up to a minute: 120 BPM.

check.q: Why count more than once?
choices: Repeated measurements that agree are easier to trust
The first count is always wrong
check.why: Repeating a measurement helps catch small mistakes.

check.q: You count 20 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate?
check.why: 20 times 4 is 80 beats per minute.

lessons.title: Bars and Counting to Four
lessons.mainIdea: Music groups beats into bars; most popular music counts four beats in each bar.
reading: Beats are easier to follow in groups. Musicians gather them into *bars*, also called measures. In most pop, hip hop and house music, each bar has four beats. You count them: one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four.

The first beat of each bar, the one, often feels strongest. It is where a new idea tends to start. The pattern of how many beats are in each bar is the *time signature*. Four beats per bar is written 4/4, and it is so common that people call it common time.

Not all music counts in four. A waltz counts in three: one, two, three. Some music from the Balkans and from India uses longer, uneven groups. Counting is a tool. Once you can count the bars, you can tell where you are in a song, just like a map tells you where you are on a street.

words.d: a group of beats that repeats in music; also called a measure
a sign that tells how many beats are in each bar, such as 4/4

look.title: Counting a Chorus
look.text: A song plays at 120 BPM in 4/4 time. The chorus lasts 8 bars. Each beat is half a second long.
look.prompt: How many beats are in the chorus? How many seconds does the chorus last?

check.q: In 4/4 time, how many beats are in each bar?
check.why: The top number in 4/4 tells you there are four beats per bar.

check.q: Which beat usually feels strongest in a bar?
check.why: The one marks the start of each bar and often gets the strongest accent.

check.q: A waltz is counted one, two, three. How many beats are in each bar?
check.why: A waltz has three beats in each bar.

lessons.title: Sixteen Steps in a Bar
lessons.mainIdea: A drum machine cuts one bar of four beats into 16 equal steps, four steps for each beat.
reading: A drum machine has a row of 16 buttons. Each one is a *step*. Together they make one bar. Since the bar has four beats, each beat gets four steps. Steps 1, 5, 9 and 13 land right on the four beats. The steps in between fall on the quick counts you can say as one-e-and-a, two-e-and-a.

Turn a step on, and the drum plays at that moment. Turn it off, and that moment is silent. The machine moves through the steps in order, then loops back to step 1. This loop is a *sequencer*: a tool that plays events in a set order, again and again, perfectly on time.

The steps are equal slices of time. At 120 BPM, one beat lasts 0.5 seconds, so each step lasts 0.5 divided by 4, which is 0.125 seconds. The whole bar of 16 steps lasts 2 seconds. Change the tempo and every step stretches or shrinks together, so the pattern keeps its shape.

words.d: one of the equal slices of time in a drum machine's bar; a bar of 4/4 usually has 16
a tool that plays sounds in a set order, looping on time

look.title: One Step at Different Tempos
look.cite: Worked out as 60,000 divided by BPM, divided by 4 steps, rounded
look.prompt: What happens to the length of one step as the tempo goes up? How long is a whole bar at 150 BPM?

check.q: On a 16-step drum machine, which steps land on the four main beats?
check.why: Each beat has four steps, so the beats start on 1, 5, 9 and 13.

check.q: At 120 BPM, how long does one step last?
check.why: One beat is 0.5 seconds, and there are four steps per beat.

check.q: What does a sequencer do?
choices: Plays sounds in a set order, looping on time
Changes the pitch of a song
check.why: A sequencer steps through a pattern in order and repeats it.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Kick, Snare and Hi-Hat
lessons.mainIdea: Most beats are built from three roles: a low kick, a sharp snare and a quick hi-hat, each placed on certain steps.
reading: Listen closely to most beats and you will hear three main parts. The *kick drum* is the low thump. The snare is the sharp crack. The *hi-hat* is the quick tick or tss. Each one has a job, like players on a team.

A classic pattern goes like this. The kick plays on steps 1 and 9, the one and three. The snare plays on steps 5 and 13, the two and four. The hi-hat plays on every odd step, 1, 3, 5 and so on, eight times per bar. Say it out loud: boom, tss, crack, tss, boom, tss, crack, tss.

House music often puts the kick on all four beats, steps 1, 5, 9 and 13. People call that four on the floor. Hip hop often moves the kick around between the beats, which gives it a bounce. Small changes in where the drums land change how a beat feels in your body.

words.d: the low, deep drum sound, often on the main beats
a pair of small cymbals that make a short tick or tss sound

look.title: Build It in Your Head
look.text: Picture 16 boxes in a row. Fill in K for kick in boxes 1, 5, 9 and 13. Fill in S for snare in boxes 5 and 13. Leave the rest empty.
look.prompt: What style of beat is this pattern closest to? What would change if you took the kick out of boxes 5 and 13?

check.q: Which drum is the low thump?
check.why: The kick drum makes the deep, low sound.

check.q: Kick drum on steps 1, 5, 9 and 13. What is this called?
check.why: A kick on all four beats is known as four on the floor, common in house music.

check.q: In the classic pattern, where does the snare usually play?
check.why: The snare on two and four, steps 5 and 13, is the classic backbeat.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Swing: Stretching Every Other Step
lessons.mainIdea: Swing delays every second step a little, turning a stiff, even rhythm into one that bounces.
reading: Play a hi-hat on all 16 steps and you get tick-tick-tick-tick, perfectly even. It can sound stiff, like a robot. Now nudge every second tick a little later. The first tick in each pair gets longer, the second gets shorter. The rhythm starts to lope. That is *swing*.

Jazz musicians have swung for more than a hundred years. Early drum machines added a swing setting to copy that human feel. The machine measures swing as a percentage. At 50 percent the steps are even. At about 66 percent, the first step of each pair takes up about two thirds of the pair, and the groove bounces hard.

Swing shows something important about rhythm. The *groove*, the feel that makes you move, can come from tiny shifts in time, less than a tenth of a second. Your brain notices these shifts even when you cannot name them. Try the swing button on the Drum Machine and listen to the same pattern change its whole mood.

words.d: a rhythm where every second step is played a little late, giving a bouncing feel
the feel of a rhythm that makes people want to move

look.title: Even or Swung?
look.text: Two versions of the same hi-hat pattern play at 90 BPM. In version A, all ticks are equally spaced. In version B, every second tick comes a bit late. Most listeners say version B makes them want to nod their head.
look.prompt: What changed between A and B? Did the tempo change? Explain.

check.q: What does swing do to a rhythm?
choices: Plays every second step a little late
check.why: Swing delays every other step to give a bouncing feel.

check.q: On a drum machine, what does 50 percent swing mean?
choices: The beat is half as fast
check.why: At 50 percent, each pair of steps is split evenly, so there is no swing.

check.q: Where did the idea of swing come from before drum machines?
choices: Jazz musicians playing with a bouncing feel
check.why: Swing is a long jazz tradition that drum machines were built to copy.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Why a Steady Pulse Helps
lessons.mainIdea: People naturally sync their movements to a steady beat, and a predictable pulse can help the body and brain settle and focus.
reading: Put on a song and watch a room. Heads nod, feet tap, and often nobody decided to do it. Moving in time with a beat is called *synchronizing*. People do it from a young age, and it gets stronger with practice. Rowers pull together. Marchers step together. Dancers at the Warehouse moved together.

Scientists who study the brain find that hearing a steady beat activates areas that plan movement, even when you sit still. The brain starts to predict when the next beat will come. When it guesses right, that can feel satisfying. That may be part of why a steady pulse feels good.

A steady pulse can also be a tool. Some people focus better with a quiet, steady beat in their headphones. Some people rock, tap or bounce a knee to think. That movement is the body finding its own rhythm, and it can help. Therapists use rhythm to help people walk more evenly after an injury and to practice speech. A beat is something the body understands.

words.d: to move or happen at the same time as something else
to say what will happen next based on a pattern

look.title: The Walking Beat
look.text: A physical therapist plays a steady click at a comfortable walking pace. A patient learning to walk again after an injury tries to step on each click. Over several weeks, her steps become more even.
look.prompt: Why might a steady beat make stepping easier? What does the brain get from the click?

check.q: What does it mean to synchronize with a beat?
choices: To stop moving when the beat starts
To move at the same time as the beat
check.why: Synchronizing means lining your movement up with the pulse.

check.q: Why might a steady beat feel satisfying?
choices: The beat makes the room warmer
The beat blocks all other sounds
The brain predicts the next beat and gets it right
The ear only hears steady sounds
check.why: The brain enjoys a pattern it can predict.

check.q: A student bounces a knee while solving a problem. What is a helpful way to see this?
choices: The body is finding a rhythm that can help thinking
It means the student is not paying attention
It always shows the student is upset
It stops the brain from working
check.why: Many people think better with movement. A steady rhythm can help focus.

lessons.title: Rhythms in Nature
lessons.mainIdea: Nature is full of rhythms that can be measured, and some of them change in a predictable way.
reading: Beats are not only made by people. Crickets chirp in rhythm. Frogs call in turns. Fireflies in some places flash together. Your heart keeps its own tempo, faster when you run, slower when you rest. These are *natural rhythms*.

In 1897, a physics teacher named Amos Dolbear wrote about crickets. He noticed that crickets chirp faster when the air is warmer and slower when it is cooler. A cricket's body warms and cools with the air, so its muscles work faster in the heat. Dolbear turned the chirp rate into a way to estimate temperature.

Scientists still use this idea. The chirp tempo is a *variable* that changes along with another variable, temperature. When two things change together in a steady way, you can use one to predict the other. You will do the same with your own beats in Chapter 64.

words.d: a repeating pattern in nature, like a heartbeat or a cricket's chirp
something that can change or be changed in an investigation

look.title: The Cricket Thermometer
look.text: Dolbear wrote that the rate of a cricket's chirp depends on the temperature, and gave a rule for finding the temperature by counting chirps for one minute.
look.cite: Amos Dolbear, The Cricket as a Thermometer, The American Naturalist, 1897
look.prompt: What two variables did Dolbear connect? How could you check his idea on a summer night?

check.q: What did Dolbear notice about crickets?
choices: They chirp faster when it is cooler
They chirp faster when it is warmer
check.why: Warmer air lets the cricket's muscles work faster, so it chirps faster.

check.q: Which is a natural rhythm?
check.why: A heartbeat is a repeating pattern made by the body, not by a machine.

check.q: Your heart rate is higher after running. What changed?
choices: Your heart stopped having a beat
The tempo of your heartbeat went up
The pitch of your heart changed
Your heartbeat became a wave in the air
check.why: Running speeds up your heart, a higher tempo.

lessons.title: When a Beat Becomes a Note
lessons.mainIdea: A click repeated faster than about 20 times a second stops sounding like a rhythm and starts sounding like a pitch.
reading: Here is a strange fact that joins this chapter to the last one. Take a single click and repeat it 4 times a second. You hear a fast rhythm. Repeat it 10 times a second and it becomes a buzz of clicks. Repeat it more than about 20 times a second, and your brain stops hearing separate clicks. You hear a low tone.

Why? A click repeated 100 times a second is a vibration at 100 Hz. That is a frequency, and frequency is pitch. The difference between a rhythm and a note is only speed. Rhythm lives at slow repetition rates. Pitch lives at fast ones. The *threshold* between them sits around 20 per second.

So a beat at 120 BPM is a very slow vibration, 2 per second. A bass note at 110 Hz is the same idea sped up 55 times. Musicians and scientists both work with repeating patterns in time. They just work at different speeds.

words.d: the point where one thing changes into another
how many vibrations or waves happen each second

look.title: Speeding Up the Click
look.text: A computer plays a click once per second, then 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 times per second. Listeners say when it stops sounding like clicks.
look.prompt: Around what rate do you predict listeners will hear a tone? What pitch would 100 clicks per second make?

check.q: A click repeats 100 times a second. What do you hear?
choices: A low tone at about 100 Hz
check.why: Above about 20 per second, repeats blend into a pitch.

check.q: What is the only real difference between a rhythm and a pitch?
check.why: Slow repeats sound like rhythm, fast repeats sound like pitch.

check.q: A beat is at 120 BPM. How many times per second does it repeat?
check.why: 120 beats divided by 60 seconds is 2 per second.

choices: An event that repeats at an even spacing in time
review.why: A beat repeats evenly, like a clock tick.

review.q: At 60 BPM, how long does each beat last?
review.why: 60 seconds divided by 60 beats is one second each.

review.q: A 16-step bar in 4/4 gives each beat how many steps?
review.why: 16 steps divided by 4 beats is 4 steps per beat.

review.q: Kick on 1 and 9, snare on 5 and 13. On which beats is the snare?
review.why: Steps 5 and 13 are beats two and four.

choices: The timing of every second step
review.why: Swing plays every second step a little late.

review.q: A cricket chirps faster. According to Dolbear, what likely changed?
Clicks repeat 200 times a second. What do you hear?
choices: A slow beat you can dance to
